common_name: Beni Shogun Fuji Apple (Low-Chill Early-Ripening Pink-Blushed Fuji Sport)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring; not self-fruitful, plant with another low-chill apple such as Anna or Dorsett Golden for pollination. Beni Shogun Fuji needs only about 500 chill hours, well below the 550-600 hours standard Fuji requires.

directions: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Beni Shogun Fuji, a pink-blushed sport of standard Fuji, needs roughly 500 chill hours rather than the 550 to 600 hours true Fuji requires, letting it flower and fruit more reliably in gardens at the warmer edge of apple-growing range where standard Fuji sets an uneven crop. It ripens about a month earlier than standard Fuji, with the same sweet, crisp, juicy flesh but a slightly deeper pink blush over the yellow skin. Thin fruit to one per cluster in late spring to improve size, and pick when fully colored for the best sweetness.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Harris County Fruit and Nut Variety List

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, fertile loam in full sun; plant with a second pear cultivar such as Hood or Flordahome for cross-pollination. Spalding is recommended by LSU AgCenter for southern Louisiana, ripening mid-September and useful for extending the Hood/Flordahome harvest window.

directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, fertile loam in full sun; Spalding is explicitly recommended by the LSU AgCenter for southern Louisiana home orchards, prized for its fire-blight tolerance in the humid Gulf South and for ripening in mid-September, later than early-season selections like Hood and Flordahome, which extends the fresh pear harvest into fall. Fruit is used both fresh and for canning, with the firm, gritty texture typical of Southern-adapted pear selections bred more for reliability than the buttery texture of European dessert pears. Prune out and destroy any blighted shoots promptly and avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer, which encourages the soft new growth fire blight favors. Harvest while still firm, then ripen off the tree at room temperature.
sources: LSU AgCenter — Choose a Pear Variety Suited to Our Climate

common_name: Douglas Pear (Fire-Blight-Tolerant Texas Home Orchard Pear)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, fertile loam in full sun; plant with a second pear cultivar such as Kieffer, Orient, or Garber for cross-pollination. Douglas is listed by the Texas Plant Disease Handbook alongside Kieffer, Orient, and Garber as moderately fire-blight-tolerant and recommended for Texas home orchards.

directions: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Douglas is grouped with Kieffer, Orient, and Garber as a moderately fire-blight-resistant Southern pear recommended for Texas home orchards by the Texas Plant Disease Handbook, tolerating the humid conditions that make European dessert pears difficult to grow without heavy spraying. Fruit has the firm, somewhat gritty texture typical of Southern-adapted pears, well suited to canning and preserving as well as fresh eating once fully ripened off the tree. Long-lived, vigorous trees are productive for decades under low-spray conditions. Harvest when fruit begins to soften at the blossom end, then ripen at room temperature for the best texture.

common_name: Carrick Pear (University of Tennessee Fire-Blight-Resistant Pear)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, fertile loam in full sun; plant with a second pear cultivar such as its companion release Morgan for cross-pollination. Carrick was released from the University of Tennessee's 1950s fire-blight-resistant pear breeding program.

directions: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Carrick was released alongside its companion selection Morgan from the University of Tennessee's dedicated 1950s fire-blight-resistant pear breeding program, developed specifically to give Southern home orchardists pear options that could withstand the fire blight pressure of humid summers without heavy spraying. Fruit has the firm, reliable qualities typical of Southern-bred pears, suited to fresh eating once ripened off the tree as well as canning and preserving. Long-lived, vigorous trees are productive for decades under low-spray conditions typical of home orchard management. Harvest when fruit begins to soften at the blossom end, then ripen at room temperature.
sources: University of Tennessee historic pear breeding bulletins

common_name: Morgan Pear (Highly Fire-Blight-Resistant University of Tennessee Pear)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, fertile loam in full sun; plant with its companion release Carrick for cross-pollination. Morgan was rated highly resistant to fire blight in USDA Beltsville, Maryland evaluations.

directions: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Morgan, the companion release to Carrick from the University of Tennessee's 1950s fire-blight-resistant pear breeding program, was rated highly resistant to fire blight in USDA Beltsville, Maryland evaluations, making it one of the more dependable pear choices for humid Southern gardens where fire blight regularly damages susceptible European cultivars. Fruit has the firm, reliable qualities typical of Southern-bred pears, suited to fresh eating once ripened off the tree as well as canning and preserving. Long-lived, vigorous trees are productive for decades under low-spray conditions typical of home orchard management. Harvest when fruit begins to soften at the blossom end, then ripen at room temperature.
sources: University of Tennessee historic pear breeding bulletins
